The valiha is the tube zither of Madagascar, a chordophone, Hornbostel-Sachs number 312.11. It is made from a bamboo tube, usually with 21 to 24 strings plucked with the fingernails; the strings were once cut from the bamboo itself and raised on gourds or wooden bridges for tuning, and today bicycle brake cable, guitar strings or piano strings are used. Malagasies regard it as the national instrument; under Merina rule, long fingernails plucked at the strings were a mark of the nobility, and it was used for leisure music and for ritual music that calls the spirits.
瓦麗哈琴為馬達加斯加弦鳴樂器，發聲分類312.11，以竹筒張弦彈撥。來源提到它除: The valiha is a Malagasy chordophone, sounding classification 312.11, with strings stretched on a bamboo tube and plucked. The source mentions that besides leisure music it is used for ritual music that calls the spirits; the recordings of the twentieth-century player Rakotozafy were mostly made live in the central recording studio of Malagasy radio; today, strung with guitar or piano strings, it can be heard in churches and folk ensembles.
瓦麗哈琴為馬達加斯加的管狀齊特琴，被視為國家樂器，發聲分類為弦鳴，Hornbos: The valiha is the tubular zither of Madagascar and is regarded as the national instrument, a chordophone, Hornbostel-Sachs 312.11. The word valiha also refers to related zithers of different shapes and materials. It is often thought locally to come from King David and is tied to the narrative of the Jewish origin of the Malagasy. Under Merina rule the instrument had high status, and keeping a long thumbnail to pluck the strings was seen as what marked a noble off from a labourer. Besides entertainment it is used in ritual music that summons spirits. Modern making uses bamboo with longer internodes, and the strings have changed from strips of bamboo to bicycle brake cable, or guitar and piano strings.
瓦麗哈琴琴身以竹製成，早期使用特定竹種，現代多選節間較長的竹材，竹管直徑約五至十: The body of the valiha is bamboo; early instruments used a particular species, and today bamboo with longer internodes is preferred, the tube about five to ten centimetres in diameter and thirty-five to one hundred and eighty centimetres long. The number of strings is usually twenty-one to twenty-four; in the old way they were cut from the bamboo itself and raised on small gourds or wooden bridges that also served as movable tuners. Modern strings are commonly unwound bicycle brake cable fixed with nails; more formal players may use guitar or piano strings instead. The marovany variant is box-shaped, with a body of wood or metal plate.
瓦麗哈琴音色溫潤而富有穿透力，兼具明亮與柔和的雙重特質。其竹製筒體結構使聲音具有: The valiha has a warm, carrying timbre that is both bright and soft. Its bamboo tube gives the sound its own resonance: the bass is warm and deep, the middle and treble clear and lively. The range is wide, from the low resonances to the high harmonics. When plucked, the sound rises and falls in waves, and because many strings vibrate at once it forms a rich layering. Compared with the brilliance of the Western harp, the valiha is more inward and mysterious; compared with the metallic quality of the guzheng, it has the warmth of natural bamboo. Its resonance uses the cavity of the bamboo tube, so the sound extends and rings, and it suits the ethereal, meditative atmosphere of ritual music.
